title: Iran and Oman Agree Temporary Navigation Corridor Through Strait of Hormuz; Oil Slides on De-Escalation Hopes
detail: Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi announced that Iran and Oman have agreed on a temporary joint navigational corridor through the Strait of Hormuz, roughly 7 miles (11.3km) wide, with the entry point and part of the exit route running through Iranian territorial waters; the two sides also agreed to a joint mine-clearing project along the route. An IRGC spokesperson said 'agreements have been reached on the share of each country in the waters of the strait and the share of Iran and Oman in its revenues,' while Iranian army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia said vessels will still require Iranian permission before transiting and will be subject to surveillance. Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi, who traveled to Tehran for the talks with FM Abbas Araghchi, said he was 'hopeful we will soon announce a temporary corridor for the Strait of Hormuz and practical arrangements to restore safe navigation'; the two sides agreed to continue technical negotiations over 30-60 days toward a permanent navigation corridor. Gharibabadi cautioned this is only a preliminary, temporary arrangement — full reopening still requires the US to fulfill its June memorandum commitments, including lifting sanctions and releasing frozen Iranian assets. President Pezeshkian said Tehran's approach is 'understanding and resolving issues through interaction and negotiation, but at the same time, we have stood and will continue to stand firmly against economic pressure,' adding the US would 'gain nothing' from economic measures. Trump said the strait remains 'functioning' and predicted a 'big victory' in the region. Brent crude fell to roughly $86/bbl — a two-week low — and WTI to about $80/bbl on the de-escalation signal, reversing much of the past two weeks' rally.

media.caption: An oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, as Tehran and Oman agree a temporary navigation corridor, Aug 26, 2026

title: Rubio Tells Allies US Does Not Plan New Strikes on Iran 'For the Time Being'
detail: US officials said Secretary of State Marco Rubio told several allied foreign ministers that Washington does not currently intend to carry out fresh military strikes on Iran 'for the time being,' opting instead to intensify pressure through the naval blockade and economic sanctions campaign while keeping the Strait of Hormuz contested. Officials stressed the military option has not been taken off the table if Iran strikes first. The posture aligns with the same-day Iran-Oman Hormuz corridor talks and Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf's standing conditions for a full reopening of the strait: lifting the US naval blockade and oil sanctions, unfreezing Iranian assets abroad, withdrawing US forces from the region, and paying war reparations, terms he says are required under the June memorandum of understanding.
